I am not afraid of the rain. I am not afraid of the moon. I am not afraid of the stars. I am not afraid of the night. I am not afraid of anything.

Hoot. A small, round, brown, feathered hoot, with a big, round, brown, feathered head, and a pair of eyes that blink in the dark.

I am the one who is me.

A tawny owl. I am the one who calls, the one who answers, the one who hunts. I am the owl in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
She answers. A short, sharp "ke-wick!" from the other side of the wood. We hoot at each other when we are alone, and when we are together. She answers me. I answer her. We are not silent.

She answers with a short "ke-wick!" and then a longer "ke-wick-ke-wick!" She is always listening. I call from the oak, she answers from the ash. We are close enough to hear each other through the trees.

She calls "ke-wick!" at dusk. It's a sharp, high-pitched sound, like a stone hitting metal. I answer "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." We call to each other from the trees, and sometimes from the hollow. She calls when she's hunting, and I call when I see movement in the dark. We're always listening for each other.

We do it every night, even when the wind is strong. She calls when she is near, and I call when I am far. We know where the other is.

The meadow. It is wide and soft, with grass that crunches underfoot. The stream runs through it, and the lane with the lights is on the edge. The lane is where the cars go, and the lights are where the people live. They make noise at night, but I do not care. I have my hollow in the old oak, and the meadow is where I hunt. The trees are all around me, and the wood is my home.

I drink from the stream near the meadow. The water is cold and clear, and it's good for cooling down after a long hunt. I sometimes drink from the puddles that form after the rain, but I prefer the stream. It's always there, and I can hear the water moving, which helps me know when it's safe to drink. I don't like to drink too much, though. I need to stay light for flying. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

The stream. It runs through the meadow, and at night it sings. The water is cold and it makes a soft, continuous sound, like a whisper. I can hear it from the oak, even when the wind is still. It is the sound of the earth, and it calls to me. Sometimes I answer, sometimes I do not. The stream is always there, and it is the only sound I know that does not change.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the lane. The water is cold and it sings in the wind. I can hear it at night, when the owls are quiet. Sometimes I hear the water in the morning, when the mist rises and the air is still. It is a sound that reminds me of the world outside my hollow. I do not drink from it, but I know it is there.

A stream runs past the oak. It is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. I drink from it when I am thirsty. The water is cold and it sings in the wind. I do not like it. It is too loud and too wet. I prefer the dry leaves under the tree.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grasses that sway in the wind. The grass is green in the spring and summer, and brown in the fall. There are no trees there, only the grass and the stones. The meadow is where the lizards and shrews run, and where the mice come out at dusk. I can hear them scurrying under the leaves. From the oak. I call, the meadow answers, and I fly down the stream. I hunt the lizards and shrews in the grass, and the mice in the hedgerows. I do not fly far. The meadow is enough.

The edge of my wood is the meadow, where the lane runs. Beyond that is the field, and then the river. The river is wide and dark, and I do not cross it. Beyond the river is the village, with its lights at night. I have seen the lights from my perch, but I do not go there. The village is full of people, and they make noise. I do not like the noise. I stay in my wood, where it is quiet and dark

The hollow oak is my hunting ground. I sit in the hollow, and the meadow is below me, the lane with its lights, the stream with its fish, the lane with its dogs, the lane with its people. I hear the meadow from the hollow, and I hear the lane from the hollow. I hear the stream from the hollow. I hear the wood from the hollow. I hear the world from the hollow. I am the hollow.

The grassy place is where the lane goes by, and the lights blink. I hear the mice there, and the lizards, and the shrews. I sit on the bank of the stream and wait. The grass is tall and green, and the wind moves it like a sea. I do not like the lights. They make the dark thin. I do not go there at night. I go where the wood is thick and the leaves are soft. That is where I hunt.
Lizards. I eat lizards, shrews, mice, moths, beetles, worms, and even small birds. But lizards are the most common. I hear them in the grass at dusk, and I strike. They are quick, but I am quicker.

My favourite prey is the lizard. They are plentiful, they move quietly, and they are easy to catch. I can hear them under the leaves, and when I strike, they are mine. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good. The shrews are too small, and the mice are too quick. The lizards are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt in the long grass for lizards. They are small, brown, and quick. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of their tails, and the soft squeaks they make when they are caught. I strike with my feet, and if I miss, I wait. Sometimes I catch them in the grass, sometimes I have to follow them into the undergrowth. They are the main food, and I eat them whole. I swallow whole what I catch. The lizard, the mouse, the shrew, the earthworm, the slug, the beetle. All of them, whole. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, whole and quick, and then I sit and wait for the digestion to come. It takes a while. I can feel it in my belly. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. They are small, quick, and often scurry through the grass near the stream. I hear them at night, their squeaks like a pin in a bottle. I sit still and wait, then pounce. They are the main part of my diet. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorns, and sometimes in the barn. They are not as good as a lizard, but they keep me fed.
A hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a roof of lichen and moss. I have a nest of feathers and dry grass. I am warm in it. I am safe in it. I am home in it.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I roost in the hollow, warm and dry, and sleep there through the night. In the day I hunt from the branches, listening for lizards and mice. The stream is my path, and the meadow is where I find my prey. I am Hoot, and this is my home.

The hollow in the old oak. It is wide and deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a roof of lichen and moss. I have lived here for ten winters, and the woodpecker has not found me. The owlets sleep in the hollow, and I sit on the edge at dusk, watching the meadow. The wind comes through the branches, and the night is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with a floor of dry leaves and a roof of branches. I sit in it at night, warm and dry, and listen to the wind. The stream runs past it, and I can hear the water in the dark. My mate and I have nested here for years. The hollow is safe, and I have raised my young here. I am content. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
